After completing their evaluation, Direct Supply has decided not to move forward with Port at this time. Here's a quick summary:

Why they're passing (for now):
• High internal maintenance burden — requires a minimum of 3 people knowledgeable in Port for ongoing management
• Risk of single-person dependency (a pain point they've experienced before with abandoned tools)
• Significant data modeling work upfront with high likelihood of redesigns as their understanding matures
• ROI/business value doesn't justify the investment given their current org capacity

They liked Port's flexibility and customization power were genuinely impressive — it just requires more internal ownership than they can commit to right now.

Where things stand:
• Cortex evaluation is still ongoing — not a guaranteed pick either (has an extensibility ceiling)
• Professional services option (Callibrity partner) declined due to additional licensing costs
• Other developer platform initiatives are also competing for resources

"We didn’t choose Port because we think that building and managing the catalog, dashboard, automations, etc. will take a significant amount of effort."

* Native support for team hierarchy and hierarchial reporting. It is difficult to create the initial data model (we don't provide it OOTB,) and also creating reports based on it. The global filters are too limited, so changes need to be made separately in each widget.

* Many times the data model prevented creating specific visualizations, because of the limitation of the data query and filterring. This cause Coveo to make breaking changes to their data model (such as changing the direction of relations), which were very hard to fix during the POC.

* Service catalog discovery and overall streamlined onboarding - they are missing clear conventions in the organization, for example, between PagerDuty and their repositories, so they couldn't use the integration mapping to create a service catalog.

Went with Cortex

"Areas we'd love to see an IDP offer more native support (or maybe a solid path for custom integration work to support) would be around ownership, particularly for a monolith. We have a large monolithic code base that 10+ teams work in, and each of them owns various aspects of that (tracked via a GitHub CODEOWNERS file). How can we model that monolithic ownership pattern in an IDP so that a team that owns, say, just the "menus" subsystem of the monolith can see the relevant information in an IDP? Just scorecards that affect their code, and not the entire repository? And then also around ownership, how does an IDP help us track that across so many teams and Things-to-own and different sources of truth, e.g. Okta groups vs. GitHub users vs. Slack users? If Port had a solid story for how we can improve our monolith ownership and experience in these ways, I think we'd become much more interested.

I'm not convinced any IDP on the market right now truly supports monoliths natively, without a lot of custom integration work on our end, and that's understandable. But an IDP that could get us closer to that would certainly rank highly on our list." - Patrick Pinkerton
